# gpcn_vpc_vpn_connection (Resource)

A VPN connection is an encrypted IPsec tunnel between a VPC in GPCN™ (Global Private Cloud Network™) and a peer gateway at your site. Once it's up, the VPC and the peer networks behind your gateway reach each other as if they shared one private network.

Manages a site-to-site VPN connection between a GPCN™ VPC and a peer gateway. The VPN connection runs on the VPN gateway of the VPC, so create the VPN gateway first. Your organization needs the Site-to-Site VPN feature, and the data center of the VPC must offer site-to-site VPN. The API key needs vpc:read to read a VPN connection, vpc-vpn-connection:create, vpc-vpn-connection:update and vpc-vpn-connection:delete to manage one, and vpc-nsg:update to create or change one, because the VPN connection adds rules to the security groups of the VPC. GPCN™ never returns the pre-shared key, so Terraform can't detect a change made outside Terraform. Set the key with psk, or with psk_wo and psk_wo_version (Terraform 1.11 or later). Every attribute changes in place except vpc_id and vpn_gateway_id.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Example: A site-to-site VPN connection for a GPCN™ VPC
#
# A VPN connection joins the VPN gateway of a VPC to a peer gateway at your
# site. Create the VPN gateway first. Your organization needs the Site-to-Site
# VPN feature, and the data center must offer site-to-site VPN.

terraform {
  required_providers {
    gpcn = {
      source  = "Global-Private-Cloud-Network/gpcn"
      version = "~>1.6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "gpcn" {
  host = "https://api.gpcn.com"
}

# The pre-shared key, 16 to 64 printable ASCII characters. A write-only
# attribute needs Terraform 1.11 or later.
variable "vpn_psk" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}

# Raise this number to send the current key to GPCN™ again.
variable "vpn_psk_version" {
  type    = number
  default = 1
}

# Lookup data center in Central US region
data "gpcn_datacenters" "central_us" {
  country_name = "United States"
  region_name  = "Central"
  name         = "Chicago 1"
}

resource "gpcn_vpc" "example" {
  name          = "terraform-demo-vpc"
  datacenter_id = data.gpcn_datacenters.central_us.datacenters[0].id
  cidr          = "10.60.0.0/16"
}

resource "gpcn_vpc_subnet" "example" {
  vpc_id = gpcn_vpc.example.id
  name   = "terraform-demo-web"
  cidr   = "10.60.1.0/24"
}

resource "gpcn_vpc_vpn_gateway" "example" {
  vpc_id     = gpcn_vpc.example.id
  depends_on = [gpcn_vpc_subnet.example]
}

resource "gpcn_vpc_vpn_connection" "example" {
  vpc_id         = gpcn_vpc.example.id
  vpn_gateway_id = gpcn_vpc_vpn_gateway.example.id
  name           = "terraform-demo-branch-office"

  # The public address of the peer gateway, and the networks behind it
  peer_address = "203.0.113.10"
  peer_cidrs   = ["192.168.10.0/24"]

  # Terraform never stores a write-only key in the plan or the state
  psk_wo         = var.vpn_psk
  psk_wo_version = var.vpn_psk_version

  # Instead of the two lines above, psk stores the key in state, marked
  # sensitive:
  # psk = var.vpn_psk
}

# Give this address to the administrator of your peer gateway
output "gpcn_vpc_vpn_connection_local_endpoint_address" {
  value = gpcn_vpc_vpn_connection.example.local_endpoint_address
}

# Configure these networks at your peer gateway
output "gpcn_vpc_vpn_connection_local_networks" {
  value = gpcn_vpc_vpn_connection.example.local_networks
}
```

## Before you start

A VPN connection needs these in place:

- A VPN gateway that's `ready`. Reference its `id` from `vpn_gateway_id`, as the example does, and Terraform builds the VPN gateway first and deletes it last.
- At least one subnet in the VPC.
- The Site-to-Site VPN feature on your organization, and a data center that offers site-to-site VPN. Check `vpn_capable` on `gpcn_vpc` or on the `gpcn_datacenters` data source.
- An API key with `vpc:read`, `vpc-vpn-connection:create`, `vpc-vpn-connection:update`, `vpc-vpn-connection:delete` and `vpc-nsg:update`. The last one is there because a VPN connection edits your security groups (see below).

When the apply finishes, give `local_endpoint_address` to the administrator of your peer gateway, and have them configure `local_networks` at their end.

## Pre-shared key

Both ends of the tunnel need the same pre-shared key. It's 16 to 64 printable ASCII characters, with no spaces, double quotes or backslashes. Set it one of two ways, and exactly one:

- **`psk`** stores the key in your state file, marked sensitive. Change `psk` to rotate the key.
- **`psk_wo`** is write-only: Terraform sends it to GPCN™ and never stores it in the plan or the state. It needs Terraform 1.11 or later, and it comes with `psk_wo_version`. Terraform can't see a change in a write-only value, so raise `psk_wo_version` to send the current `psk_wo` again and rotate the key.

GPCN™ never returns the key, and the provider doesn't write it to its logs. That means Terraform can't tell if someone changed the key outside Terraform.

## Security group rules

A VPN connection opens the tunnel's traffic for you. For each peer network, it adds an ingress rule for all protocols to every security group that's bound to a subnet in the VPC. Each rule's description names the connection, and GPCN™ removes them when you delete it.

`gpcn_vpc_nsg` leaves those rules out of its `rule` set, so they never show up as a difference, and it sends them back unchanged whenever it replaces a group's rules. If you write a rule with the same direction, protocol, ports and remote CIDR yourself, give it a description of your own. It then becomes yours, and the connection no longer manages it or removes it. A rule you copy exactly, description included, stays the connection's.

If you create a connection, or change its peer networks, while an update of a `gpcn_vpc_nsg` is replacing that group's rules, the group can lose the connection's rule, and the connection won't add it back. To restore it, replace the connection with `terraform apply -replace`, declare the rule in `gpcn_vpc_nsg`, which makes it part of that group's rule set, or recreate the group and then make a full update of the connection.

A security group you bind to a subnet after the connection exists doesn't get the rules right away. It gets them on the connection's next full update, which is any change other than `name` or `description` alone. Raising `psk_wo_version` or editing a peer network counts, for example.

## Peer networks

`peer_cidrs` lists the networks behind your peer gateway, one to ten blocks with a prefix length from /8 to /32. Write each one as its network address, such as `192.168.10.0/24`. GPCN™ rewrites a block that has host bits set, which would make every plan show a change, so Terraform refuses `192.168.10.7/24` at plan time and tells you the right form.

The blocks can't overlap each other, the VPC, or the peer networks of another VPN connection. `peer_address` must be a public IPv4 address.

## Connection state

`state` is one of `creating`, `connecting`, `connected`, `disconnected`, `error`, `failed` or `removing`. GPCN™ updates it when it reads the peer gateway, so it can change without a change in your configuration.

- `disconnected` is normal for a tunnel with no traffic. It isn't a fault.
- Terraform doesn't wait for `connected`. The apply finishes when GPCN™ has built the VPN connection, because a tunnel only comes up when the peer gateway answers.
- `failed` means the last job failed. `failure_reason` says why, and a create that ends there leaves the resource tainted, so the next apply creates it again.

If `desired_applied` is false, the settings GPCN™ saved aren't the ones the data center is running yet. Terraform shows a warning when it refreshes a VPN connection whose saved settings the data center isn't running and that has no job running. If the data center couldn't apply saved settings, the next plan shows an update that sends them again.

A connection that failed and can't be updated is replaced: Terraform deletes it and creates it again.

If a create times out, you interrupt it, or GPCN™ gives an unclear answer and already has the connection, Terraform marks the connection tainted, and the next apply replaces it. To keep it instead, wait until GPCN™ finishes, then run `terraform untaint <address>`. If the provider can't check for the connection after an unclear answer, it saves nothing, and the error says a connection may exist.

## Limits

- GPCN™ allows 4 VPN connections per VPC by default. Connections in the `failed` and `removing` states count.
- Each VPN connection takes one peer gateway address, and a VPC can't have two connections to the same address.
- An `appliance` VPN gateway allows 10 peer networks across all the VPC's connections.
- The name must be unique within the VPC.

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Name of the VPN connection, 1 to 63 characters: letters, digits, spaces, dots and hyphens, starting and ending with a letter or digit. It must be unique within the VPC
- `peer_address` (String) Public IPv4 address of the peer gateway, the device at your site at the other end of the tunnel. Private, shared, loopback, link-local and multicast addresses are refused
- `peer_cidrs` (Set of String) The peer networks: 1 to 10 IPv4 CIDR blocks reachable through the peer gateway, each with a prefix length from /8 to /32. Write each block as its network address, such as 192.168.10.0/24, because GPCN™ rewrites a block with host bits set. The blocks must not overlap each other, the VPC, or the peer networks of another VPN connection
- `vpc_id` (String) Unique identifier of the VPC the VPN connection belongs to. Changing this value requires replacing the VPN connection
- `vpn_gateway_id` (String) Unique identifier of the VPN gateway of the VPC. It must be the VPN gateway of vpc_id. Referencing the VPN gateway resource makes Terraform create the VPN gateway first and delete it last. Changing this value requires replacing the VPN connection

### Optional

> **NOTE**: [Write-only arguments](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/resources/ephemeral#write-only-arguments) are supported in Terraform 1.11 and later.

- `description` (String) Additional information about the VPN connection, up to 500 characters as the API counts them (UTF-16 code units)
- `dh_group` (Number) Diffie-Hellman group for the IKE exchange: 2, 5 or 14. GPCN™ uses 14 when omitted
- `dpd` (Boolean) Whether dead peer detection is on. When on, GPCN™ probes the peer gateway every 30 seconds and restarts the VPN connection after 120 seconds without an answer. GPCN™ turns it on when omitted
- `encryption` (String) Encryption algorithm: 'aes128', 'aes192' or 'aes256'. GPCN™ uses 'aes256' when omitted
- `ike_lifetime_seconds` (Number) Lifetime of the IKE security association in seconds: 60 to 86400, a multiple of 60. GPCN™ uses 28800 when omitted
- `ike_version` (String) Version of the IKE protocol: 'v1' or 'v2'. GPCN™ uses 'v2' when omitted
- `integrity` (String) Integrity algorithm: 'sha256', 'sha384' or 'sha512'. GPCN™ uses 'sha256' when omitted
- `ipsec_lifetime_seconds` (Number) Lifetime of the IPsec security association in seconds: 60 to 86400, a multiple of 60. GPCN™ uses 3600 when omitted
- `pfs_group` (Number) Diffie-Hellman group for perfect forward secrecy, which is always on: 2, 5 or 14. GPCN™ uses 14 when omitted
- `psk` (String, Sensitive) Pre-shared key, 16 to 64 printable ASCII characters with no spaces, double quotes or backslashes. Terraform stores it in state, marked sensitive. Set exactly one of psk and psk_wo. Changing psk sends the new key to GPCN™
- `psk_wo` (String, Sensitive, [Write-only](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/resources/ephemeral#write-only-arguments)) Pre-shared key, write-only: Terraform never stores it in the plan or the state. It needs Terraform 1.11 or later and psk_wo_version. Same format as psk. Set exactly one of psk and psk_wo. Terraform sends the key on create, and again when psk_wo_version changes
- `psk_wo_version` (Number) Version of psk_wo. Terraform can't see a change in a write-only value, so raise this number to send the current psk_wo to GPCN™ and rotate the key. It's null after an import, so the first apply sends the key again

### Read-Only

- `desired_applied` (Boolean) Whether the connection's saved settings are what the data center is running. It's false while saved settings are not yet applied, for example during an update or after one that failed
- `failure_reason` (String) Why the last operation on the VPN connection failed, or null when none has. It changes when an operation fails or succeeds
- `gateway_kind` (String) How the data center provides the VPN gateway: 'router' or 'appliance'
- `id` (String) Unique identifier for the VPN connection in UUID format
- `local_endpoint_address` (String) The VPN gateway address: the public IPv4 address your peer gateway connects to
- `local_networks` (List of String) The networks on the GPCN™ side of the VPN connection, as CIDR blocks. Configure them at your peer gateway. The list changes when the subnets of the VPC change
- `state` (String) Lifecycle state of the VPN connection: one of 'creating', 'connecting', 'connected', 'disconnected', 'error', 'failed' or 'removing'. It changes when GPCN™ reads the peer gateway. A VPN connection with no traffic rests in 'disconnected', which is not a fault

## Import

Import is supported using the following syntax:

The [`terraform import` command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) can be used, for example:

```shell
# The import ID is the ID of the VPC and the ID of the VPN connection, joined by
# a slash. The key is not imported, so the first apply sends it again.
terraform import gpcn_vpc_vpn_connection.example "c13808d9-3b7d-42c5-a21d-f0961308a38a/8f1a2b3c-4d5e-6f70-8192-a3b4c5d6e7f8"
```

GPCN™ never returns the key, so `psk` and `psk_wo_version` are null after an import. Whichever your configuration sets, the first apply sends the key again.
